title: Feelings, precisely
goal: Name feelings with the precision Indonesians use among friends: the grades of annoyance (*kesal, jengkel, dongkol*), the untranslatable *gemas* and *gregetan*, relief (*lega*), being moved (*terharu*), and the difference between *rindu* and *kangen*. Then say what caused the feeling, and how strongly.
bekal: grade annoyance from *kesal* to *dongkol* to *marah*, and say who or what it is aimed at
link a feeling to its cause: *bikin aku gemas*, *sampai nangis*, *jadi terharu*, *gara-gara…*

notes: **Gemas and gregetan.** *Gemas* is the overwhelming urge to squeeze or pinch something unbearably cute — babies, kittens, chubby cheeks — and English has no single word for it. It also covers exasperation: *gemas lihat dia lambat banget*. *Gregetan*, from Javanese, is the same itch with more impatience. The standard spelling is *gemas*; you will see *gemes* everywhere online.

**Kesal, jengkel, dongkol.** Three grades of annoyance. *Kesal* is the general “annoyed”; *jengkel* is more irritated, often at something repeated; *dongkol* is resentment kept inside, simmering. Rina climbs the ladder in two lines and then tells us she kept it in — which is exactly what *dongkol* means.

**Dipendam** — “buried” — is what you do with feelings you don't express: *memendam perasaan*, *rindu yang terpendam*. Indonesian culture values keeping the peace, so *dipendam* is common; the healthy release is *curhat* (from *curahan hati*, “pouring out the heart”) to a friend.

**Lega** is relief: the weight lifted after a worry ends, a debt is paid, an argument is resolved. *Rasanya lega banget* is the classic phrase. Casual speech also says *plong* (“clear, unblocked”): *Hatiku jadi plong.*

**Terharu** is the feeling of being moved, usually to the edge of tears, by something kind or beautiful. It is positive, and *nangis karena terharu* (crying because you're moved) is common at weddings and graduations. *Sampai* (“to the point of”) marks how far the feeling went: *aku sampai nangis*.

**Galau and ketahuan.** *Galau* is a mix of restless, confused and sad, the default mood of love songs and Monday mornings; the word is old (KBBI glosses it as a troubled, muddled mind), but its second life as slang made it a national favourite. *Ketahuan* is “found out, caught”: *Ketahuan, ya* is the rueful admission that someone has read you correctly.

grammars.title: Annoyed, by degrees
body: Indonesian distinguishes annoyance more finely than English does, and the grade you choose tells the listener how seriously to take you. From mildest to strongest:
after: The target takes *sama* in speech (*kesal sama dia*) and *kepada* or *terhadap* in writing (*kesal kepadanya*). For a situation or an event, use *atas* or *dengan*: *geram atas keputusan itu*.

⚠️ *Marah* is a strong word in Indonesia, where showing anger openly costs face — yours more than the other person's. Saying *Saya agak kesal* when you are furious is not dishonest; it is the local scale.

grammars.title: What caused it: bikin, membuat, sampai, jadi, gara-gara
body: Naming the feeling is half the job; the other half is saying what caused it and how far it went. These are the patterns, casual first.
after: *Jadi* before a feeling marks the feeling as a reaction to what was just said: *Wah, saya jadi malu* (“now you've made me embarrassed”). You will hear it constantly in polite conversation, usually in response to a compliment.

dialogs.intro: A few days later, a Wednesday, eight in the evening. The office is almost empty. Fajar, packing up, notices Sarah staring at her screen without typing.

notes: **Bengong** is staring blankly, lost in thought — the body is at the desk, the mind in Melbourne. The standard word is *melamun* (to daydream). *Jangan bengong!* is what you say to someone who has missed their turn at the traffic lights.

**Rindu and kangen** both mean “to miss, to long for”. Fajar's explanation is exactly right: *rindu* is the word of poetry, songs and formal writing (*rindu kampung halaman*), *kangen* the word of WhatsApp and phone calls. As a verb with an object, standard Indonesian uses *merindukan*: *Saya merindukan keluarga.*

**Jangan-jangan** — literally “don't, don't” — introduces a suspicion, often a worried or teasing one: “I bet…”, “what if…”. *Jangan-jangan dia lupa* (“don't tell me he's forgotten”). It is always about a possibility you half expect.

**Gorengan jam empat sore.** Homesickness in Indonesian is described through small sensory details, and afternoon *gorengan* — fried tofu, tempeh, banana fritters from a street cart — is the Jakarta equivalent of Sarah's flat white. Saying you would miss it is a compliment to the city, and Fajar hears it that way.

**Kata nenek saya** (“my grandma says”) is the standard way to introduce home-grown wisdom. The advice itself — eat first, sadness needs energy — is pure Indonesian care, the same instinct behind the A1 greeting *Sudah makan?*

**Saya jadi terharu.** *Jadi* before the feeling makes it a reaction to what Fajar just did. Sarah then immediately says she will still check the report — the Indonesian way of accepting kindness without letting the moment get too heavy.

grammars.title: Near-twins: feelings that look alike
body: Dictionaries often give these pairs the same English translation. They are not interchangeable; pick the wrong one and you will sound either stiff or strangely dramatic.

head: Pair
The difference
rows: afraid (of something present) / worried (about what might happen)
embarrassed, ashamed / reluctant out of respect

after: *Sakit hati* is strong: it means someone wounded you and you may not forgive easily. *Kecewa* is what you say to a colleague whose report was late; *sakit hati* is what you say to a friend who betrayed a secret.

blocks.text: Positive feelings are where Indonesian is most generous with nuance. These are the words you need to congratulate, thank and comfort people properly.

*Bangga pada* or *bangga akan* in writing, *bangga sama* in speech: *Saya bangga pada diri sendiri* (“I am proud of myself”). ⚠️ *Puas* is “satisfied”, not “pleased with yourself” in the smug sense; for that, Indonesians say *besar kepala* (B1 Unit 15).

sections.title: Feelings in casual and Gen-Z speech

blocks.text: Young Jakarta has its own emotional vocabulary, much of it now used by everyone under fifty. Recognise all of these; use them only with friends.

head: Casual
Meaning
Nearest standard
rows: on the verge of tears, weepy

blocks.text: *Ambyar* is Javanese for “scattered into pieces”; the late singer Didi Kempot made it the national word for heartbreak, and his fans still call themselves *Sobat Ambyar*. *Baper* you met in Unit 8 and Unit 14; it is the most useful word on this list.
Cover the Indonesian column, read the English, and rebuild each sentence from memory.

rows: Sarah, I've read your draft speech. The content is good, but the opening is too short.
*Sarah, draf sambutanmu sudah saya baca. Isinya bagus, tetapi pembukaannya terlalu singkat.*
At an official event the important guests are addressed first, in order from the highest rank down.
*Di acara resmi, tamu-tamu penting disapa lebih dulu, urut dari jabatan yang paling tinggi.*
Right. And the greeting? The students and their parents come from all sorts of religions.
*Baik. Lalu salamnya? Peserta dan orang tuanya berasal dari berbagai agama.*
Then I'll go with the second. After the greeting, does there have to be the “praise and thanks” part?
*Kalau begitu saya pilih yang kedua. Sesudah salam, apakah harus ada “puji syukur”?*
Understood. I'll write the ending out in full: the apology, the thanks, then the greeting.
*Mengerti, Pak. Penutupnya akan saya tulis lengkap: permohonan maaf, terima kasih, lalu salam.*
